signals.title: What Patients Say They Can't Access: Mining Cancer Screening Barriers from Online Communities
signals.summary: Cancer screening disparities persist across the U.S., yet the patient-reported barriers driving low uptake remain poorly characterized at scale. While clinical surveys capture structured responses, they miss the organic, unsolicited discourse where patients candidly describe real-world obstacles.
signals.implication: High relevance to C2A2 operations; include in next leadership brief.
signals.long_summary: Cancer screening disparities in the U.S. continue, but the barriers patients face are not well understood on a large scale. Traditional clinical surveys provide structured responses but overlook the natural, unsolicited discussions where patients express their real-world challenges. This understanding of patient-reported barriers is crucial for addressing the low uptake of cancer screenings. This research matters for the community seeking to stay informed about AI, as it highlights the importance of mining conversational data to uncover insights that structured data may miss, ultimately leading to improved healthcare outcomes.

signals.title: Latency-Aware Adaptive Best-of-$N$
signals.summary: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language model responses by spending additional computation at inference time, and the right amount of compute depends on the prompt. Adaptive TTC methods allocate compute based on signals of response quality such as observed rewards, often by stopping once the signal exceeds a fixed threshold, and generally measure cost by the number of generations or tokens.
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: Test-time compute (TTC) enhances language model responses by allowing for additional computation during inference, with the required amount varying depending on the input prompt. Adaptive TTC methods distribute computational resources based on indicators of response quality, such as observed rewards, and typically cease computation when the quality signal surpasses a predetermined threshold. These methods usually assess cost in terms of the number of generations or tokens produced. Understanding the development of adaptive TTC techniques can be significant for a community engaged in AI, as it highlights the ongoing efforts to improve response quality in language models while optimizing resource use.

signals.title: Source-balanced Capped Fisher: Bounded Evidence Aggregation for User Inference in Language Models
signals.summary: User inference asks whether a source contributed documents to a language-model update, even when the auditor observes only fresh documents from that source. Document-level scores can provide evidence of participation, but combining this evidence is challenging: documents differ in baseline predictability and in how strongly they reflect information learned from other documents of the same source.
signals.implication: Update constitutional clauses and compliance mappings for community operators.
signals.long_summary: User inference investigates whether a particular source has contributed to the documents used in a language model's update, despite the auditor only seeing new documents from that source. The challenge lies in aggregating document-level scores that indicate participation, as these documents vary in baseline predictability and the extent to which they represent information learned from other documents from the same source. This highlights the complexities involved in accurately determining the influence of different sources on language model updates. Understanding these dynamics is important for our community as it emphasizes the need for reliable methods in tracing source contributions, which is crucial for maintaining accountability and transparency in AI developments.

signals.title: Matriarchy Classics: A Computational Approach to Swap Only Gendered Words in Classic Novels
signals.summary: This paper proposes a trustworthy computational method to gender-swap public domain novels, with programmatic guarantees that only gendered words are inverted and all other words are left unchanged. This may seem like a simple task, but both large language models and naive rule-based methods fail to complete it.
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: This paper introduces a reliable computational technique designed to swap only gendered words in public domain novels while ensuring that all other words remain unchanged. The authors assert that, although the task may appear straightforward, existing large language models and basic rule-based approaches are inadequate to achieve this goal effectively. The development of this method highlights the intricacies involved in manipulating linguistic structures while preserving the original text's integrity. This matters for a community keeping up with AI as it emphasizes the ongoing challenges in natural language processing and the importance of precision in AI applications.

signals.title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer
signals.summary: Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-model Transfer (PACT), a form of latent communication between language models, combines a larger model's prompt representations with a smaller model's efficient generation, offering a promising way to balance capability and inference cost. However, existing systems provide limited support for independently evaluating large-small model collaboration, and improved task performance alone does not establish whether the receiver benefits from the sender's information.
signals.implication: Prioritize provenance checks and misinformation/abuse response protocols.
signals.long_summary: Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-model Transfer (PACT) is a method that facilitates communication between language models by integrating prompt representations from larger models with the efficient generation capabilities of smaller models. This approach aims to strike a balance between enhanced performance and reduced computational costs. However, current systems face challenges in evaluating collaborations between large and small models independently. Additionally, simply improving task performance does not ensure that the smaller model benefits from the information provided by the larger model. Understanding PACT is essential as it highlights both potential advancements and inherent limitations in AI model collaboration, which are crucial for the community to navigate the evolving landscape of AI capabilities and implications.

signals.title: TrustMix: Graceful Degradation for Pretrained Models under Distribution Shift
signals.summary: Predicting beyond the training domain necessarily requires assumptions about how the ground truth extrapolates, yet in most neural networks these assumptions are made only implicit through the architecture. We propose TrustMix, a lightweight post-hoc method that makes a pretrained model's extrapolative behaviour explicit and controllable.
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: TrustMix is a new method designed to enhance pretrained models' ability to predict beyond their training domains. The approach addresses the challenge of how models handle distribution shifts by making the assumptions regarding their extrapolative behavior explicit and manageable. Rather than relying solely on implicit architectural features, TrustMix provides a framework that allows for better control over how the models operate when presented with data that diverges from what they have previously encountered. This development is crucial for a community that needs to keep pace with AI, as it highlights the importance of understanding and managing model behavior in real-world applications where data can vary significantly from training conditions.

signals.title: Backbone-Informed Adaptation after EEG Pretraining: A Capacity-Controlled Study
signals.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models learn representations that combine information across channels and time. This structure motivates adapters that model the same relationships during downstream learning.
signals.implication: Track for context; no immediate governance action required.
signals.long_summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are designed to learn representations that integrate information across different channels and time. This inherent structure in EEG models supports the development of adapters that aim to replicate these relationships during subsequent learning tasks. The study suggests that by utilizing such adapters, the efficiency of downstream learning can be enhanced. Understanding how EEG data can inform model adaptation is relevant for the community as it emphasizes the importance of effective representation learning in improving AI models’ capabilities and performance.

signals.title: Structural Conditional Independence Test via Neural Quantile Resolution
signals.summary: Conditional independence testing is difficult when dependence is weak, localized, or expressed through distributional changes rather than a global mean shift. Existing tests usually return a scalar statistic or p-value, which summarizes evidence against independence but does not describe where the conditional law changes.
signals.implication: Update constitutional clauses and compliance mappings for community operators.
signals.long_summary: Conditional independence testing poses challenges, particularly when the dependence is weak, localized, or manifests through distributional changes instead of a global mean shift. Current testing methods typically yield a scalar statistic or p-value, which indicates evidence against independence but fails to pinpoint where the conditional law is altered. This has implications for the effectiveness of AI systems that rely on accurate modeling of independence among variables. Understanding these nuances in independence testing is crucial for community members, as it enhances their grasp of the limitations and advancements in AI methodologies.

signals.title: Depth or Description? When a One-Step Latent Score Replaces Lookahead in Proactive Information Acquisition
signals.summary: A proactive agent must decide what to ask before it acts. Exact lookahead values combinations of questions but is expensive and leans on a fitted model; a one-step score is cheap but can miss them.
signals.implication: Reassess role boundaries and human override for community deployments. Monitor adoption pressure and revise formation cadence for tool onboarding.
signals.long_summary: A proactive agent is faced with the challenge of determining what questions to ask before taking action. The traditional method of using exact lookahead values allows for combinations of questions but can be costly and relies heavily on a pre-fitted model. Alternatively, a simpler approach utilizing a one-step score is less expensive but may overlook critical combinations of inquiries. This comparison highlights the trade-offs between depth and efficiency in information acquisition. Understanding these dynamics is important for our community as it illustrates the complexities involved in optimizing decision-making processes within AI systems.
